chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.summary: Anatomically modern humans are estimated to have first arrived on the Indian subcontinent between 73,000 and 55,000 years ago. The earliest known human remains in South Asia date to 30,000 years ago.

events.label: 1200 BC
events.text: The Iron Age in the Indian subcontinent from about 1200 BCE to the 6th century BCE is defined by the rise of Janapadas, which are realms, republics and kingdoms—notably the Iron Age kingdoms of Kuru, Panchala, Kosala, and Videha.

events.label: 600 BC
events.text: The period from c. 600 BCE to c. 300 BCE featured the rise of the Mahājanapadas, sixteen powerful kingdoms and oligarchic republics in a belt stretching from Gandhara in the northwest to Bengal in the eastern part of the Indian subcontinent—including parts of the trans-Vindhyan region.

events.label: 413 BC
events.text: The Haryanka dynasty was overthrown by the Shaishunaga dynasty (c. 413–345 BCE).

events.label: 322 BC
events.text: The Maurya Empire (322–185 BCE) unified most of the Indian subcontinent into one state, and was the largest empire to exist in South Asia.

events.label: 185 BC
events.text: The Maurya Empire would collapse in 185 BCE, on the assassination of the then-emperor Brihadratha by his general Pushyamitra Shunga.

events.label: 8th c.
events.text: Islamic conquests made limited inroads into modern Afghanistan and Sindh as early as the 8th century, followed by the invasions of Mahmud Ghazni.

events.label: 11th c.
events.text: The Chola Empire conquered southern India in the 11th century and were known for their art and architecture.

events.label: 14th c.
events.text: The empire declined in the late 14th century following the invasions of Timur and saw the advent of the Malwa, Gujarat, and Bahmani sultanates, the last of which split in 1518 into the five Deccan sultanates.

events.label: 16th c.
events.text: The early modern period began in the 16th century, when the Mughal Empire conquered most of the Indian subcontinent, signaling proto-industrialisation and becoming the biggest global economy and manufacturing power.
The British Indian Empire was partitioned in August 1947 into the Dominion of India and Dominion of Pakistan, each gaining its independence.

chapters.narrative: Anatomically modern humans are estimated to have first arrived on the Indian subcontinent between 73,000 and 55,000 years ago, with the earliest known remains dating to 30,000 years ago [S1]. The Iron Age from about 1200 BCE saw the rise of Janapadas such as Kuru, Panchala, Kosala and Videha, followed by the Mahājanapadas from c. 600 BCE to c. 300 BCE stretching from Gandhara to Bengal [S1]. The Maurya Empire unified most of South Asia from 322 to 185 BCE before collapsing after Brihadratha's assassination by Pushyamitra Shunga [S1]. Later periods included Islamic conquests in the 8th century, Chola rule in the 11th century, and Mughal dominance from the 16th century, until partition in August 1947 into India and Pakistan [S1].

chapters.title: Classical period (c. 200 BCE – 650 CE)
chapters.summary: The time between the Maurya Empire in the 3rd century BCE and the end of the Gupta Empire in the 6th century CE is referred to as the "Classical" period of India. The Gupta Empire (4th–6th century) is regarded as the Golden Age of India, although a host of kingdoms ruled over India in these centuries.

events.label: 3rd c. BC
events.text: The time between the Maurya Empire in the 3rd century BCE and the end of the Gupta Empire in the 6th century CE is referred to as the "Classical" period of India.

events.label: 1st c. BC
events.text: The territory of the empire covered large parts of India from the 1st century BCE onward.

events.label: 1st c.
events.text: The Kushan Empire expanded out of what is now Afghanistan into the northwest of the Indian subcontinent under the leadership of their first emperor, Kujula Kadphises, about the middle of the 1st century CE.

events.label: 3rd c.
events.text: By the 3rd century, their empire in India was disintegrating and their last known great emperor was Vasudeva I.
Kadambas originated from Karnataka, was founded by Mayurasharma in 345 CE which at later times showed the potential of developing into imperial proportions.

events.label: 4th c.
events.text: Samudragupta's 4th-century Allahabad pillar inscription mentions Kamarupa (Western Assam) and Davaka (Central Assam) as frontier kingdoms of the Gupta Empire.

events.label: 5th c.
events.text: The latter Guptas successfully resisted the northwestern kingdoms until the arrival of the Alchon Huns, who established themselves in Afghanistan by the first half of the 5th century CE, with their capital at Bamiyan.

events.label: 6th c.
events.text: After the downfall of the prior Gupta Empire in the middle of the 6th century, North India reverted to smaller republics and monarchical states.

Ruled by three dynasties Varmanas (c. 350–650 CE), Mlechchha dynasty (c. 655–900 CE) and Kamarupa-Palas (c. 900–1100 CE), from their capitals in present-day Guwahati (Pragjyotishpura), Tezpur (Haruppeswara) and North Gauhati (Durjaya) respectively.

events.label: 13th c.
events.text: The Kamarupa kingdom came to an end in the middle of the 13th century when the Khen dynasty under Sandhya of Kamarupanagara (North Guwahati), moved his capital to Kamatapur (North Bengal) after the invasion of Muslim Turks, and established the Kamata Kingdom.

chapters.narrative: The time between the Maurya Empire in the 3rd century BCE and the end of the Gupta Empire in the 6th century CE is referred to as the Classical period of India [S2]. The Kushan Empire expanded out of what is now Afghanistan into the northwest of the Indian subcontinent under Kujula Kadphises about the middle of the 1st century CE, and by the 3rd century their empire in India was disintegrating with Vasudeva I as last known great emperor [S2]. Samudragupta's 4th-century Allahabad pillar inscription mentions Kamarupa (Western Assam) and Davaka (Central Assam) as frontier kingdoms of the Gupta Empire [S2]. After the downfall of the Gupta Empire in the middle of the 6th century, North India reverted to smaller republics and monarchical states [S2].

chapters.title: Early medieval period (c. 650 – 1200)
chapters.summary: Early medieval India began after the end of the Gupta Empire in the 6th century CE. From the fifth century to the thirteenth, Śrauta sacrifices declined, and support for Shaivism, Vaishnavism, and Shaktism expanded in royal courts, while the support for Buddhism declined.

events.label: 6th c.
events.text: Early medieval India began after the end of the Gupta Empire in the 6th century CE.

events.label: 7th c.
events.text: The Hindu Shahi dynasty ruled portions of eastern Afghanistan, northern Pakistan, and Kashmir from the mid-7th century to the early 11th century.
Lalitaditya Muktapida (r. 724–760) was an emperor of the Kashmiri Karkoṭa dynasty, which exercised influence in northwestern India from 625 until 1003, and was followed by Lohara dynasty.

events.label: 10th c.
events.text: By the end of the 10th century, several feudatories of the empire took advantage of the temporary weakness of the Gurjara-Pratiharas to declare their independence, notably the Kingdom of Malwa, the Kingdom of Bundelkhand, the Tomaras of Haryana, and the Kingdom of Sambhar and the Kingdom of Dahala.

events.label: 11th c.
events.text: The Chola Empire emerged as a major power during the reign of Raja Raja Chola I and Rajendra Chola I who successfully invaded parts of Southeast Asia and Sri Lanka in the 11th century.
In 1097 CE, the Karnat dynasty of Mithila emerged on the Bihar/Nepal border area and maintained capitals in Darbhanga and Simraongadh.

events.label: 12th c.
events.text: During this period the other major ruling families of the Deccan, the Hoysalas, the Seuna Yadavas of Devagiri, the Kakatiya dynasty and the Southern Kalachuris, were subordinates of the Western Chalukyas and gained their independence only when the power of the Chalukya waned during the latter half of the 12th century.
The Chalukya dynasty ruled parts of southern and central India from Badami in Karnataka between 550 and 750, and then again from Kalyani between 970 and 1190.
They fell in 1324 following the invasion of Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq.

events.label: 14th c.
events.text: Under this dynasty, the Maithili language started to develop with the first piece of Maithili literature, the Varna Ratnakara being produced in the 14th century by Jyotirishwar Thakur.

chapters.narrative: Early medieval India began after the end of the Gupta Empire in the 6th century CE [S3]. From the fifth century to the thirteenth, Śrauta sacrifices declined and support for Shaivism, Vaishnavism, and Shaktism expanded in royal courts while support for Buddhism declined [S3]. The Hindu Shahi dynasty ruled portions of eastern Afghanistan, northern Pakistan, and Kashmir from the mid-7th century to the early 11th century [S3]. Lalitaditya Muktapida (r. 724–760) was an emperor of the Kashmiri Karkoṭa dynasty, which exercised influence in northwestern India from 625 until 1003 [S3]. The Chola Empire emerged as a major power during the reign of Raja Raja Chola I and Rajendra Chola I who successfully invaded parts of Southeast Asia and Sri Lanka in the 11th century [S3].

chapters.title: Late medieval period (c. 1200 – 1526)
chapters.summary: The late medieval period is marked by repeated invasions by Muslim Central Asian nomadic clans, the rule of the Delhi Sultanate, and by the growth of other states, built upon military technology of the sultanate. The Delhi Sultanate was a series of successive Islamic states based in Delhi, ruled by several dynasties of varying origins.

events.text: The sultanate was the only Indo-Islamic state to enthrone one of the few female rulers in India, Razia Sultana (r. 1236–1240).

events.label: 13th c.
events.text: The empire rose to prominence as a culmination of attempts by the south Indian powers to ward off Islamic invasions by the end of the 13th century.

The Vijayanagara Empire was established in 1336 by Harihara I and his brother Bukka Raya I of Sangama dynasty, which originated as a political heir of the Hoysala Kingdom, Kakatiya Empire, and the Pandyan Empire.
In the south, the Bahmani Sultanate in the Deccan, born from a rebellion in 1347 against the Tughlaq dynasty, was the chief rival of Vijayanagara, and frequently created difficulties for them.
The sultan's army was defeated on 17 December 1398.

Starting in 1490, the Bahmani Sultanate's governors revolted, their independent states composing the five Deccan sultanates; Ahmadnagar declared independence, followed by Bijapur and Berar in the same year; Golkonda became independent in 1518 and Bidar in 1528.
Lodi rule lasted in Delhi until the defeat of the last sultan, Ibrahim Khan Lodi, in 1526 to the forces of Babur.
Although generally rivals, they allied against the Vijayanagara Empire in 1565, permanently weakening Vijayanagar in the Battle of Talikota.
The Aravidu dynasty successors ruled the region but the empire collapsed in 1614, and the final remains ended in 1646, from continued wars with the Bijapur sultanate and others.
It lasted until 1646, although its power declined after a major military defeat in 1565 by the combined armies of the Deccan sultanates.

chapters.narrative: The late medieval period is marked by repeated invasions by Muslim Central Asian nomadic clans, the rule of the Delhi Sultanate, and by the growth of other states, built upon military technology of the sultanate [S4]. The sultanate was the only Indo-Islamic state to enthrone one of the few female rulers in India, Razia Sultana (r. 1236–1240) [S4]. The Vijayanagara Empire was established in 1336 by Harihara I and his brother Bukka Raya I of Sangama dynasty [S4]. In the south, the Bahmani Sultanate in the Deccan, born from a rebellion in 1347 against the Tughlaq dynasty, was the chief rival of Vijayanagara [S4]. Lodi rule lasted in Delhi until the defeat of the last sultan, Ibrahim Khan Lodi, in 1526 to the forces of Babur [S4].

chapters.title: Early modern period (1526–1858)
chapters.summary: The early modern period of Indian history is dated from 1526 to 1858, corresponding to the rise and fall of the Mughal Empire, which inherited elements from the Timurid Renaissance. During this age India's economy expanded, relative peace was maintained and arts were patronised.

events.text: Hyderabad was founded by the Qutb Shahi dynasty of Golconda in 1591.
In 1737, the Marathas defeated a Mughal army in their capital, in the Battle of Delhi.
In 1739, Nader Shah, emperor of Iran, defeated the Mughal army at the Battle of Karnal.

events.label: 18th c.
events.text: The Kingdom of Mysore in southern India expanded to its greatest extent under Hyder Ali and his son Tipu Sultan in the later half of the 18th century.

The company's victory under Robert Clive in the 1757 Battle of Plassey and another victory in the 1764 Battle of Buxar (in Bihar), consolidated the company's power, and forced emperor Shah Alam II to appoint it the diwan, or revenue collector, of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.
The Maratha–Mysore War ended in April 1787, following the finalising of treaty of Gajendragad, in which Tipu Sultan was obligated to pay tribute to the Marathas.

In 1817, the British went to war with the Pindaris, raiders who were fled in Maratha territory, which quickly became the Third Anglo-Maratha War, and the British government offered its protection to the Rajput rulers from the Pindaris and the Marathas.

With the decline of the Sikh Empire, after the First Anglo-Sikh War in 1846, under the terms of the Treaty of Amritsar, the British government sold Kashmir to Maharaja Gulab Singh and the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, the second-largest princely state in British India, was created by the Dogra dynasty.
However, Kashmir was immediately sold under the Treaty of Amritsar (1850) to the Dogra dynasty of Jammu and thereby became a princely state.
The Indian Rebellion of 1857 was a large-scale rebellion by soldiers employed by the British East India Company in northern and central India against the company's rule.

During this age India's economy expanded, relative peace was maintained and arts were patronised [S5]. Hyderabad was founded by the Qutb Shahi dynasty of Golconda in 1591 [S5]. In 1737, the Marathas defeated a Mughal army in their capital, in the Battle of Delhi, and in 1739 Nader Shah, emperor of Iran, defeated the Mughal army at the Battle of Karnal [S5]. The Kingdom of Mysore in southern India expanded to its greatest extent under Hyder Ali and his son Tipu Sultan in the later half of the 18th century [S5].

chapters.title: Independence and partition (1947–present)
chapters.summary: In particular, the partition of the Punjab and Bengal led to rioting between Hindus, Muslims, and Sikhs in these provinces and spread to other nearby regions, leaving some 500,000 dead. The police and army units were largely ineffective.

chapters.narrative: The partition of the Punjab and Bengal led to rioting between Hindus, Muslims, and Sikhs in these provinces and spread to other nearby regions, leaving some 500,000 dead [S6]. The police and army units were largely ineffective during this violence [S6]. This period also saw one of the largest mass migrations anywhere in modern history, with a total of 12 million Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims moving between the newly created nations of India and Pakistan [S6]. India and Pakistan gained independence on 15 and 14 August 1947 respectively [S6]. The excerpts provided offer only a limited perspective on these events and do not represent all points of view [S6].
